messages.subject: Riparian Sampling
parts:
Hello everyone,

I have been assessing riparian bird community responses to different
disturbance types (fire and forestry) at the wetland riparian/forest
edge in the Boreal Plain ecozone of western Canada. The non-forested
riparian area varies from 5-20m wide. I used a combined line
transect/point-count sampling technique where I employed a 400m transect
along the riparian/forest edge. Species were grouped into one of 5
distance intervals from the survey line (0-10, 10-25, 25-50, 50-100,
> >100m) on either the waterside or forested side. Two point counts were
placed 50m from the water's edge usually into the upland and at 50 and
350m along the transect . Species detected at point counts were placed
into distance from observer bands and time intervals (i.e. for removal
models). Because of the high number of species, the number of
individuals detected and the habitat type, using a distance estimator
(e.g. range finder) to get exact distances was both impractical and
impossible.

I understand sampling along riparian edges, as I have, violates the
assumptions of distance sampling. However, sampling perpendicular to the
riparian edge reduces the power I would have to detect differences and
significantly reduce the number of sites I would be able to sample.
Furthermore, I am, after all, interested in birds at the ecotone. I have
forest inventory data (GIS) for each 'detection band' for both the
transects and point counts and can estimate area of 'riparian', forest
type and percent disturbance by forestry or fire at each interval. Is it
possible to use vegetation as a covariate and use birds found only on
one side of the transect to estimate detection probabilities and/or
densities for species using Distance? Any other suggestions would be
helpful!

Thanks in advance,

Kevin Kardynal (MSc candidate)
